prompt.context: Your friend Carlos wants to invest in a rafting business in California. In addition to the investment, he wants to work as general manager of this business. Carlos has asked you the following questions.
prompt.question: (1) Is the business currently profitable? (2) How much is the business worth? (3) Should Carlos acquire it?

clarifying_info.q: What are the operating hours / days of the season?
clarifying_info.a: The business is open every day in July and August, and only 2 days per week in May, June, and September. It is closed the rest of the year.

clarifying_info.q: How many boats does the business have?
How many trips does each boat make per day?
clarifying_info.a: On average 20 trips per boat per day.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price per trip?

clarifying_info.a: Labor: 4 rafting instructors at $15 per hour worked.
General manager salary: $40,000/year; 2 leased vans at $5,000/van/year; insurance: $8,000/year; overhead: $2,000/year.

clarifying_info.q: What discount rate should we use for the valuation?
What valuation method should we use?
clarifying_info.a: Use a perpetuity valuation assuming zero growth.

framework: Profitability: identify all revenue drivers (boats, trips/day, price, operating days) and all cost drivers (variable labor, fixed overhead/insurance/salaries/leases)
Compute operating days accounting for seasonal schedule (July+August every day; May/June/September only 2 days/week)
Annual profit = revenue minus total costs
Valuation: apply perpetuity formula CF/r using annual profit as proxy for cash flow
Acquisition decision: consider risks, growth assumptions, opportunity cost of capital, and business-specific vulnerabilities

questions.prompt: Question 1: Is the business currently profitable? Calculate annual revenue and costs.
questions.guidance: Candidate should methodically identify all revenue inputs (boats x trips/day x price x operating days) and all costs (variable labor hours x days, plus each fixed cost line). Strong candidates will notice the seasonal schedule requires computing operating days carefully, and will flag insurance as a non-obvious but important cost in a risky outdoor business. They should also flag the general manager salary since Carlos will take that role.

math.setup: Operating days: July + August = 60 days (2 full months); May, June, September = 2 days/week across ~12 weeks = 24 days. Total = 84 days/year. Revenue = price x trips/boat/day x boats x days. Variable cost = instructors x hourly rate x hours/day x days. Fixed cost = sum of all fixed items.
steps: Revenue: $20/trip x 20 trips/boat/day x 5 boats x 84 days = $168,000/year
Variable labor: 4 instructors x $15/hour x 8 hours/day x 84 days = $40,320 approx $40,000/year
math.answer: Annual profit approx $68,000. The business is profitable.

questions.prompt: Question 2: How much is the business worth?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use the perpetuity formula CF/r, treating operating profit as a proxy for cash flow and stating the simplifying assumptions (no taxes, no working capital adjustments, zero growth). A strong candidate will note these assumptions explicitly.

math.setup: Perpetuity value = CF / r, where CF = $68,000 and r = 10%.

questions.prompt: Question 3: Should Carlos acquire the business?
questions.guidance: Candidate should move beyond the numbers and discuss qualitative risk factors. A superior answer addresses: (a) risks inherent in the business such as weather dependence and liability, (b) realism of the zero-growth assumption, (c) opportunity cost of capital, and (d) revenue stability.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks and considerations should Carlos weigh before deciding to acquire the rafting business?

categories.name: Business risk
ideas: Outdoor adventure business is weather-dependent; bad seasons devastate revenue
Rafting carries injury/liability risk that could increase insurance costs or lead to lawsuits
Seasonal cash flow means Carlos must manage liquidity during off-season months

categories.name: Valuation assumptions
ideas: Zero-growth perpetuity may be conservative if the business can expand boats or routes
If growth is positive, the true value exceeds $680,000; if negative, it is less
Ignoring taxes overstates cash flow; after-tax profit would reduce value

categories.name: Opportunity cost
ideas: $680,000 invested elsewhere at 10% generates the same return with potentially less risk
Carlos should compare this investment against other uses of capital

categories.name: Strategic considerations
ideas: Is Carlos operationally suited to run a seasonal outdoor business?
Are there synergies or growth levers such as group packages, corporate retreats, or gear rentals?
Competitive landscape: are there other rafting operators on the same river?

recommendation: The business is currently profitable at approximately $68,000/year and valued at approximately $680,000 under a perpetuity model
Based purely on the numbers, acquisition appears viable if the purchase price is at or below $680,000
risks: Revenue is weather-dependent and inherently volatile
Liability and insurance costs could escalate given the risky nature of the activity
Zero-growth assumption may not hold; competition or market saturation could erode profits
Seasonal operation creates cash flow gaps requiring working capital management
next_steps: Negotiate purchase price relative to the $680,000 valuation baseline
Conduct due diligence on historical revenue variability and past insurance claims
Explore growth opportunities to test whether a higher perpetuity value is achievable
Assess Carlos's personal fit and operational experience for running a seasonal outdoor business
